executive_summary: CHF/JPY trades at 195.05 (5 August close), meaning one Swiss franc buys 195.05 yen, and the pair has fallen 2.72% over one month, 4.38% over three months and 2.90% over six months while still holding a 1.90% gain over twelve. That performance profile is the whole story in miniature: the franc's structural superiority over the yen delivered a year of gains, and a single week of Japanese official action plus a hawkish Bank of Japan has begun unwinding them. The dominant bilateral narrative is that this is the one G10 cross where the two standalone dossier views compound rather than cancel — the CHF dossier ranks the franc last of eleven tactically on a net score of −0.4915, the JPY dossier ranks the yen second of eleven on +0.3606, and combining a bearish base with a bullish quote produces the most negatively-signed pair in the matrix. Three bilateral differentials do not appear in either standalone view: this is the only cross in the set where the yen earns carry over the franc (+100bp, widening toward +125-150bp), so shorting CHF/JPY costs roughly 1% annualised against 3.35% for shorting AUD/JPY; the positioning spread is violently asymmetric, with the yen leg beyond its historical extreme at 185,047 contracts net short against a franc leg at only the 52nd percentile; and both officialdoms cap the pair from opposite ends, the SNB leaning against franc strength while the Ministry of Finance leans against yen weakness, leaving no official actor resisting a decline. The offsetting force is genuine and structural: both economies import essentially all their energy, but Japan's terms of trade at 83.95 against Switzerland's 100.60 mean every dollar of Brent hurts the yen roughly twice as hard, and Switzerland's AAA/37.6% sovereign against Japan's A1/187.6% is the largest credit-quality gap in the G10. We are Bearish CHF/JPY tactically at conviction 4 (net weighted score −0.3847), targeting 191.50 over two to four weeks, and Bearish strategically at conviction 2 (net score −0.1757), targeting 188.00 — the sharp conviction decay being the honest consequence of terms of trade and fiscal risk reasserting themselves at strategic weights. The caveat is specific: a Brent move above USD 115 flips this pair bullish faster than any rate differential can offset, and high oil is the key complication — a geopolitical shock can create safe-haven demand for yen, but if the same shock keeps oil high it also worsens Japan's terms of trade, which makes yen strength harder to sustain.

market_context.valuation_assessment: Both dossiers agree the pair is expensive and disagree on by how much, because they use incompatible methodologies. The CHF dossier's PPP table shows a +55.73% deviation with an implied CHF/JPY fair value of 126.0, which is a BIS real-effective-index ratio rather than an absolute parity estimate and should be treated as an ordinal signal only. The JPY dossier's relative-deviation method is more defensible: the yen is 7.7% cheap to the franc measured as the difference between each currency's percentage deviation from its own 30-month real-effective mean, implying CHF/JPY fair value of 181.13 against spot of 195.05, a 7.1% overvaluation. Japan's BIS real broad effective exchange rate is 65.30 for June 2026, the lowest reading ever recorded for the yen, while Switzerland's sits at 101.69, the 40th percentile of its window and essentially at its mean. The market is pricing this as a permanent feature rather than a deviation, and the current level embeds the assumption that a permanently-zero SNB and a Bank of Japan that stops at 1.25% is the terminal configuration — which is where the edge sits.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The carry arithmetic is the defining bilateral feature of this pair and it runs opposite to every other yen cross. The SNB policy rate is 0.00% against a Bank of Japan target of 'around 1.0 percent', so a long CHF/JPY position pays approximately -100bp annualised and a short position earns +100bp — this is the only relationship in the G10-plus-SGD set in which the yen is the higher-yielding leg. On front-end sovereign yields the gap is wider: the 2-year JGB at 1.497% against the Swiss 2-year at 0.14% is a 136bp advantage to the quote currency, and at ten years the JGB at 2.801% against the Swiss Confederation at 0.475% is 232.6bp. Carry-to-vol on the CHF dossier's 8.49% proxy for a long CHF/JPY position is -0.12, by an order of magnitude the least punitive vol-adjusted yen long available (compare -0.35 for short AUD/JPY and -0.41 for short USD/JPY). Carry is emphatically working across the risk complex but not in this pair, because CHF/JPY is a funding-currency-versus-funding-currency cross in which carry-on regimes sell both legs roughly symmetrically. The cross-implied forward path is approximately +0.84% annualised (the pair rises in the forwards), 16bp below the 100bp policy gap, the wedge attributable to SARON fixing at -0.04% and unobservable cross-currency basis on both legs. A short CHF/JPY position must overcome only 14 pips a month to break even, making the carry cost of the bearish thesis nearly negligible.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The bilateral policy differential is -100bp against the base currency and is scheduled to widen, which is the cleanest single argument for the pair falling. The SNB sits at 0.00% having constructed its own June conditional inflation forecast of 0.6%/0.6%/0.7% on the explicit assumption of a zero policy rate through 2028, while the Bank of Japan sits at 1.00% having hiked 25bp on 16 June and held 8-1 on 31 July with Takata dissenting for an immediate 1.25%. The trajectory is one-directional: OIS prices an implied BoJ rate of 1.21% after the 18 December meeting, so the differential moves from -100bp toward -121bp on market pricing alone, and toward -150bp on our expectation of 50bp of BoJ tightening by end-Q1 2027, against an SNB that cannot move because it has told the market it will not. Transmission into this specific pair is unusually direct because there is no third-currency leg to dilute it: CHF/JPY is a pure bilateral rate expression, and unlike USD/JPY it carries no offsetting Fed variable. The front end confirms the direction — the 2-year JGB at 1.497% against the Swiss 2-year at 0.14% gives a 136bp quote-leg advantage that has widened as the JGB repriced, while Swiss yields are pinned by a central bank with no scheduled meeting inside the tactical window. The pricing gap is the edge: public sources put the 18 September BoJ hike probability at somewhere between 16% and 35%, against a governor who said on 31 July that if monetary conditions are accommodative there is a chance the pace of hikes could speed up, and the JPY dossier assesses fair probability at 45-50%. Confidence is 68 rather than higher because the September meeting falls outside the tactical window and because the two public representations of BoJ pricing cannot be reconciled at the front end.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the differential is not merely wider, it is structurally divergent in a way that is rare in G10. Japan is the only economy in the set whose policy rate is unambiguously below its own central bank's neutral estimate — the June Summary of Opinions puts neutral 'at around 2 percent' against a 1.00% rate, implying 100bp of latent tightening — while Switzerland is the only economy whose central bank has publicly pre-committed to inaction for three years. The differential therefore has a mechanical floor and no ceiling: the worst case for a short CHF/JPY position is that the gap stays at -100bp, and the plausible case is -150bp to -200bp by mid-2027. Quantitative tightening reinforces the quote leg: BoJ JGB purchases step down from JPY 2.5tn monthly in Q3 2026 to JPY 2.0tn from April 2027 against redemptions of JPY 6.5-7tn a month, taking holdings from roughly JPY 518tn to a projected JPY 480tn, while the SNB's balance sheet is growing as it leans against franc strength. The honest counterweight, and it is why confidence is 66 rather than 75, is the disconfirming evidence from the last twelve months: the JGB 10-year rose roughly 122bp and CHF/JPY still gained 1.90%, because the rise in Japanese yields was a fiscal risk premium concentrated in the super-long rather than a policy premium in the front end. The resolution test is observable and pair-specific — if the next leg of the JGB move is led by the 2-year rather than the 30-year, the rate channel is working and the pair falls; if the 30-year leads, the pair rises despite the differential.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The inflation differential is the widest of any bilateral pairing in the set and it is moving further in the quote currency's favour. Swiss headline CPI was 0.5% year-on-year in June with the SNB's preferred core measure at 0.3%, against Japanese national headline of 1.7% and core of 1.6%, and — more importantly for the tactical window — Tokyo July core at 1.9% against a 1.7% consensus with core-core at 2.0%. That is a headline differential of -120bp and a core differential of -160bp against the base currency, and because Tokyo leads the national series by roughly a month, the 20 August national print is likely to widen it further. The transmission is via relative policy response: Switzerland's 0.3% core gives the SNB no reason to move in either direction, while Japan's accelerating Tokyo series gives the BoJ evidentiary cover to hike in September. Real-rate arithmetic reinforces the pair direction — the Swiss real policy rate is -0.50% against Japan's -0.70% on headline, so the nominal gap flatters the franc on a real basis, but the direction of the real gap is closing as Japanese nominal rates rise while Swiss inflation stays pinned. Growth is more balanced and mildly favours the quote leg: Swiss Q1 GDP was +0.66% quarter-on-quarter with the EY forecast cut to 0.6% for 2026 on pharmaceutical tariffs, against Japanese Q1 of +0.45% and a JCER consensus of +0.80% annualised for Q2, plus a June Tankan at +22 for large manufacturers, the highest since 2018. Asymmetric data sensitivity is decisive here: Japan's CPI moves this pair far more than Switzerland's, because the BoJ has an active reaction function and the SNB has publicly abolished its own.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the question is whether the inflation-expectations regimes have genuinely diverged, and the evidence says they have. Japan's June Tankan showed corporate price expectations at 2.7% one year ahead, 2.6% at three years and 2.6% at five, all above target and all higher than March, while the BoJ's own June household survey found 90.4% expecting higher prices over the next year, the highest since the series began in 2006. Switzerland has no comparable mechanism: the SNB's own conditional forecast is 0.6%/0.6%/0.7%, comfortably inside a 0-2% band at every horizon point, and the SFSO core measure at 0.3% shows an energy-driven headline that has not broadened. The wage channel is the clean differentiator — Japan's 2026 shunto settled at 5.01% with a 3.50% base-pay component for a third consecutive year above 5%, with five consecutive months of positive real wages, while Switzerland publishes no usable high-frequency wage series. Two offsets keep confidence at 55. First, the Japanese energy-subsidy roll-off that mechanically lifts FY2027 core is a subsidy artefact rather than demand, and the BoJ's own Outlook assumes Dubai crude falling from roughly USD 80 to USD 70 — if wrong, Japan tightens into deteriorating real income, which is franc-supportive through the growth channel. Second, Swiss headline sustaining above 1.0% with core above 0.6% would restore franc policy optionality and neutralise this factor entirely. Both are live, which is why the stance is Bearish but not high-confidence.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: CHF/JPY is the rarest configuration in G10 FX: a safe-haven-versus-safe-haven cross in which both legs are simultaneously funding currencies, which means the pair's beta to risk is structurally low and unstable in sign. Both currencies are used as safe-haven and funding currencies because of their unique characteristics and low interest rates, and the pair consequently tends to range and lacks the participation of the higher-beta yen crosses. Under the current carry-on regime — S&P 500 at 7,489.72, high-yield OAS at 284-287bp, VIX at 17.09 at roughly the 48th percentile of its one-year range, gold down 17.94% over six months — both legs are being sold as funding, which is why the pair spent July ranging while AUD/JPY trended. The bilateral question is therefore not 'does risk-off help the franc or the yen' but 'which haven has more stored energy', and the answer is unambiguous: the yen carries a 185,047-contract net short, an official buyer of last resort with roughly JPY 20tn of demonstrated firepower in 2026, and a real effective rate at an all-time low, while the franc carries a 52nd-percentile short, an official seller leaning against its strength, and a real effective rate at its mean. A risk shock therefore reprices the yen harder than the franc, which makes risk-off bearish for this pair — the inverse of the intuition that both dossiers' standalone risk sections would suggest. The stance is Neutral rather than Bearish only because the current regime is intact, there is no dated catalyst inside four weeks, and the classification flips if the shock is energy-driven rather than equity-driven.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the volatility-compression regime that has suppressed both legs is statistically unlikely to persist, and the asymmetry of the mean reversion favours the pair falling. USD/JPY realised volatility sits in the 0.5th, 10th and 9.2nd percentiles of its five-year distribution at one, three and six months respectively, and high-yield spreads are within 46bp of an all-time low — distributions this compressed revert, and when they do, the currency with the larger short and the official bid reprices further. The yen has both; the franc has neither, and in fact has an official seller. The counter-argument is genuinely strong and is why confidence is only 50: the yen's safe-haven property has been demonstrably degraded in 2026 because escalation raises the price of the oil Japan imports, and the pair rose to a 40-year yen low during a Middle East escalation that would historically have supported the quote currency. So the sign of this factor depends on the nature of the shock — an equity, credit or AI-complex shock is bearish for the pair because the yen squeeze dominates; an energy shock is bullish for the pair because Japan's terms of trade dominate. Weighting those by probability, we assess an equity/credit-led volatility event at roughly 15% and an energy-led one at roughly 18-20% over six months, which is close to balanced, but the magnitude asymmetry favours the bearish case because a 185,047-contract forced unwind moves faster and further than a terms-of-trade grind.

The net positioning differential amplifies rather than mutes the pair signal: specs are short both currencies, but the quote leg sits beyond its historical extreme threshold while the base leg sits at the statistical midpoint, so the pair-implied speculative position is effectively long CHF/JPY. strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the futures positioning differential decays to a non-signal within weeks and what replaces it is a structural flow balance that is genuinely two-sided for this pair. On the bullish-pair side, GPIF announced in May 2026 the largest reallocation in five years, seven percentage points out of JGBs into foreign equities — roughly USD 52bn of programmatic yen selling — and Japanese residents bought JPY 1.09tn of foreign long-term bonds in a single early-July week. On the bearish-pair side, none of the ten major Japanese life insurers plans to increase unhedged foreign bonds in FY2026, four intend to increase JGB holdings, and the group's FY2026 term-end USD/JPY assumption of 154 is materially stronger than spot — a standing yen bid that activates on weakness — while the franc leg faces an unmeasurable but structurally large short in cross-border bank lending and FX swaps, since ING identified on 28 July that carry investors are rotating their funding leg from yen into francs precisely because franc funding is cheaper and avoids Japanese intervention risk. That last observation is the key bilateral point: the reassignment of the funding-currency role from yen to franc is itself a persistent CHF/JPY selling flow, because it means new carry positions are financed by selling francs rather than yen. Bilateral investment linkage is real but thin: Switzerland is among the largest single sources of FDI inflows into Japan alongside Hong Kong and France, and Japan is one of the three leading global sources of FDI outflows, but neither creates a measurable high-frequency CHF/JPY flow. Netting the programmatic outflows against the insurer bid and the funding rotation gives no directional signal.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both economies import essentially all their energy, so the naive expectation is that the commodity channel nets to zero for this pair — and that expectation is wrong by a wide margin, because the intensity of the exposure is radically different. Applying the framework's direction rules: oil up is a strong negative for the yen and a mild negative for the franc, so the net effect of rising oil is CHF/JPY rising. LNG (JKM) up is strongly negative for JPY with no direct franc channel, reinforcing the same direction. Gold up is positive for CHF with no yen channel, again bullish for the pair — and gold's 17.94% six-month drawdown is currently the one commodity channel running against the pair. Quantitatively the asymmetry is stark: Japan's June mineral fuel imports were JPY 2.10tn, up 41.9% year-on-year, with petroleum import values up 59.3% and coal up 46.8% while crude volumes fell 13.7% — a pure price shock — and terms of trade collapsed from 88.34 in April to 83.95 in May, against a since-1960 average of 150.50. Switzerland's equivalent deterioration is a rise in headline CPI from 0.1% to 0.5% and terms of trade of 100.60, up from 100.00 in the prior period — an order of magnitude less damage. Bilateral trade is too small to matter as a flow channel: Swiss goods exports to Japan were USD 9.3bn in 2024 against imports of USD 7.7bn, for a net Swiss surplus of USD 1.6bn, roughly USD 17bn of two-way trade in a pair whose daily turnover dwarfs it. Tactically the factor is Bullish for the pair but at only 58 confidence and 0.06 weight, because Brent has already fallen 13% from the 23 July spike of USD 105.32 to USD 91.82, and the 19 August Japanese trade print should therefore improve.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.19 strategic weight this is the second-heaviest factor and the strongest single argument for the pair rising — it contributes +0.1178 and is the primary reason strategic conviction is 2 rather than 4. The differential is structural, not cyclical. Switzerland runs a current account surplus of 9.77% of GDP against Japan's 5.79%, and the composition matters more than the level: Switzerland's surplus rests on three independent legs (a goods surplus in pharmaceuticals and precision engineering, a services surplus in finance and commodity trading, and primary income), whereas Japan's JPY 34.52tn record surplus is generated almost entirely by primary income of JPY 42.28tn that is reinvested abroad and never repatriated, while the component that actually moves spot — the goods balance — has flipped into deficit for two consecutive months, with June at JPY 406.9bn against a JPY 120bn consensus. Creditor status is diverging: Switzerland's net international investment position is CHF 974bn and rising, while Japan has fallen to the third-largest net creditor behind Germany and China after 34 years at the top, and the yen's share of allocated global reserves fell to 5.56% in Q1 2026, down 0.25pp in one quarter. The Strait of Hormuz has not physically normalised — fewer than ten commodity ships a day were transiting on 27 July against roughly one hundred before the conflict — so the risk premium in Japan's import bill is paused rather than resolved. The counterweight is that Switzerland's own surplus is deteriorating at the margin, down CHF 11bn year-on-year in Q1, and faces a dated threat in the Section 232 pharmaceutical tariff plus a USD 200bn corporate investment pledge into the United States that is itself a multi-year franc-selling outflow. Netting, the pair-level external differential compresses but stays firmly in the franc's favour.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The guidance divergence between these two central banks is the widest in the G10 and it is one-directional for the pair. The SNB has pre-committed to inaction: its conditional inflation forecast is constructed on an explicit 0.00% policy-rate assumption through 2028, its June statement pledged an increased willingness to intervene in the foreign exchange market to counter a rapid and excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc, and late-July reporting has SNB insiders seeing zero until end-2027. The Bank of Japan has done the opposite: Governor Ueda said on 31 July that if monetary conditions are accommodative there is a chance the Bank could speed up the pace of interest rate hikes, that given underlying inflation nearing 2% the Board must focus on upside price risks, and that the Board will debate policy from the next meeting onward — while Takata dissented for an immediate 1.25%. A base currency whose central bank has abolished its own optionality against a quote currency whose central bank has just named a live meeting is definitionally a falling pair. Two bilateral features amplify this beyond what either standalone dossier captures. First, sequencing: the BoJ meets on 18 September, six days before the SNB on 24 September, so the quote leg sets the tone and the base leg can only react. Second, and more important, both official reaction functions cap this pair from opposite ends — the SNB has committed to selling francs into strength and has said nothing about buying them into weakness, while the Ministry of Finance has spent roughly JPY 20tn in 2026 buying yen into weakness and has never sold yen into strength. There is no official actor anywhere resisting a CHF/JPY decline, and two resisting a rise.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.12 strategic weight guidance becomes the binding constraint rather than context, and the asymmetry deepens. The SNB has removed itself as a source of positive surprise for three years, which converts the franc from a cyclical low-yielder into a structural funding currency — and a currency without policy optionality that also yields less than its counterparty is, by construction, the leg that gets sold. The BoJ meanwhile has delivered 100bp of cumulative tightening, published a coherent QT path, and articulated a neutral anchor of 'around 2 percent', with a member already voting for 1.25%. External validation reinforces the divergence: the US Treasury's 23 July report described substantial yen undervaluation and stated that Japanese monetary normalisation would help anchor inflation expectations and reduce excessive exchange rate volatility, while the same institution kept Switzerland on its monitoring list with Switzerland now meeting only one of three criteria — meaning the SNB is less constrained in selling francs than it was, and the MoF has tacit US cover for buying yen. Both developments are bearish for the pair. Confidence is 66 rather than higher for two symmetrical credibility risks: the SNB's January 2015 floor removal establishes that a three-person board meeting four times a year with minimal guidance can surprise discontinuously, and the Takaichi government's 352-seat supermajority on an expansionary platform is a genuine constraint on how fast the BoJ can deliver, with the Cabinet Office having asked the Bank to act while understanding initiatives taken by the Takaichi Cabinet.

The dated events are overwhelmingly quote-leg and overwhelmingly bearish for the pair: the BoJ Summary of Opinions on 10 August, Japanese June wage data on 7 August, Q2 GDP in the week of 17 August, the July trade balance on 19 August, the July national CPI on 20 August, and the Ministry of Finance intervention disclosure in the final week of August that will confirm or refute the JPY 8.45tn estimate. On the base leg the only dated events are Swiss July CPI and the manufacturing PMI in the first week of August, both of which face unfavourable energy base effects and would therefore be franc-negative if they print soft — meaning even the base-currency calendar is skewed bearish for the pair. What holds this factor at Neutral is the undated risk, which is the single largest bilateral asymmetry in the pair's event set: a Middle East re-escalation. Brent has traded from 70.46 to 126.69 to 91.82 within five months, and because Japan imports roughly 99% of its oil against Switzerland's imported-but-diversified energy mix, an energy shock is unambiguously bullish for CHF/JPY even though it would be bearish for both currencies against the dollar. Intervention risk is also two-sided but asymmetric in size: the MoF has demonstrated roughly JPY 20tn of yen buying in 2026, which is a hard floor under the quote leg, while the SNB's lean against franc strength is a soft ceiling on the base leg of a far smaller magnitude.

Those two tails are roughly comparable in probability and opposite in sign. Netting a scheduled bearish calendar against an undated bullish energy tail and two opposing idiosyncratic sovereign tails, Neutral is the honest reading at a 0.05 weight.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This factor is normally a two-sentence footnote, and for this pair it is not, because the fiscal differential is the largest in the G10 and is the documented mechanism by which the pair rose 1.90% over twelve months while the yield gap moved against it. Switzerland is rated AAA with general government debt at 37.6% of GDP and a constitutionally entrenched debt brake, and its ten-year yields 0.475%. Japan is rated A1/A+/A with central-plus-local debt revised up to 187.6% of GDP on a consolidated basis, and its 30-year yields 3.971% — within 4bp of an all-time high of 4.013% set on 9 July — with a FY2026 budget assuming a 3.0% debt-service rate, the highest in 29 years, and debt-service costs up 10.8% to JPY 31.3tn. That is a 150-percentage-point debt differential and a three-to-four-notch rating gap, and the transmission into this pair is specific: when Japanese long-end yields rise for fiscal reasons rather than policy reasons, the curve bear-steepens, the currency weakens, and CHF/JPY rises. Tactically the factor is Bullish for the pair but at only 48 confidence and 0.04 weight, because the Japanese Ministry of Finance has actively managed supply — FY2026 calendar-base market issuance was cut by JPY 3.8tn to JPY 168.5tn and new debt held below JPY 30tn for a second year — and no rating action is pending on either side inside the window.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.07 strategic weight this contributes +0.0385 and, together with Factor 5, is the reason strategic conviction is 2 rather than 4. The arithmetic worsens for the quote leg over time: Japan is entering the first period in three decades in which rising rates cost the sovereign real money, refinancing a 187.6%-of-GDP stock at progressively higher coupons while the BoJ shrinks its holdings from roughly JPY 518tn to a projected JPY 480tn by end-March 2027. A sitting policymaker has named the risk — Tamura warned that halting the taper risks purchases being perceived as fiscal financing, which could undermine the credibility of the Bank — and Ueda himself told the 31 July press conference that long-term fiscal policy must be guided in a way that maintains market trust. Switzerland faces nothing remotely comparable: the Confederation issues sparingly, sovereign CDS is effectively unquoted for lack of demand, and the debt brake has kept the budget near balance for two decades. This is a slow-burning, one-directional support for the pair, and it is the specific reason we bound the strategic downside at 180.00 — a franc that is cheap on carry does not become cheap on credit, and a yen that is cheap on valuation is cheap partly because of credit. Confidence is 55 rather than higher because the structural mitigants on the quote side are powerful: roughly 90% domestic JGB ownership, stable ratings with no agency action in 2025 or 2026, and a record current account financing the state internally.

The trend and moving-average configuration point one way: a 16-month uptrend has been broken, all three major averages are above spot and bearishly stacked, and a fresh death-cross configuration typically attracts systematic flow for months. The structural levels frame a wide range: on the downside, 192.58 then 190.00 — the level Bank of America named as its target with a stop at 206.5 — then 187.50 as the measured move from the broken 199.25-204.43 rectangle, then 185.00; on the upside, 199.25 as the defining pivot, then the 200.81-200.99 moving-average cluster, then 202.55 and 204.00. Against that, the pair has a documented multi-year tendency to mean-revert rather than trend, precisely because both legs are funding currencies: since both are funding currencies the pair tends to range quite a bit and lacks the participation of the major yen crosses, though it does carve out a trend of some sort over time. Liquidity is the binding practical constraint — it is considered a low-liquidity asset, ranks sixth in European-session trade volume, and is not recommended for beginners — which means realised volatility understates gap risk and that both authorities regularly conduct currency interventions in it. Confidence is 48 because a thin cross with a mean-reverting history and two interventionist authorities is not a reliable trend vehicle over six months.

Against that, the same abundance of dollar liquidity is what keeps the carry regime alive, and a live carry regime suppresses both legs roughly equally. Second, if reserve balances approach the Fed's minimum comfortable level and money markets tighten, the more crowded short covers harder, again the yen leg. Neither is a base case, and both are unmeasurable this cycle because the basis is unobtainable for either currency, which is why confidence is 45 rather than higher.

tactical.rationale: At tactical weights the dominant factors are Policy & Rates at 0.24, Inflation & Growth at 0.18 and Flows & Positioning at an adjusted 0.13, together carrying 55% of the weight, and all three point the same way for the pair. The reason they align is that this is the one G10 cross where the two standalone dossier views compound rather than cancel: the CHF dossier ranks the franc 11 of 11 tactically on a score of -0.4915 and the JPY dossier ranks the yen 2 of 11 on +0.3606, so combining a bearish base with a bullish quote produces the most negatively-signed pair in the entire opportunity set — and neither dossier states this in cross terms because each is written in isolation. The bilateral interaction adds three things that do not exist in either standalone view. First, the carry sign inverts: this is the only relationship in the set where the yen out-yields the franc, so shorting CHF/JPY earns +100bp instead of paying it, and the cross-implied forward path of only +0.84% annualised means a short pays away just 14 pips a month against 28 for short AUD/JPY. Second, the positioning differential amplifies rather than mutes: specs are short both currencies, but the yen leg at 185,047 contracts is beyond its extreme threshold at roughly the 4th percentile while the franc leg at 46,455 sits at the 52nd, so the pair-implied speculative position is long CHF/JPY and it is that position which the 30 July intervention forced to cover. Third, and most powerful, both officialdoms cap the pair from opposite ends — the SNB has pledged to lean against franc strength and the Ministry of Finance has spent roughly JPY 20tn leaning against yen weakness — so no official actor anywhere resists a CHF/JPY decline while two resist a rise. The genuine conflict is Factor 5: both economies import their energy, but Japan's terms of trade at 83.95 against Switzerland's 100.60 mean rising oil is bullish for the pair, and that channel is the only route by which the thesis fails quickly. What is priced versus what we expect is the tactical edge: the market prices a BoJ that stops at 1.25% with September at 16-35%, and a Swiss front end still carrying 12-25bp of hawkish premium against a bank that has ruled out moving — both errors push the same way, and the 1M cross forward outright of roughly 195.19 against our 191.50 expectation is a 369-pip gap. The path of least resistance is lower, because spot sits below all three moving averages in a bearishly stacked configuration, the 199.25 range floor and the mid-July double bottom have both failed, and the residual yen short still has to cover. Dated catalysts are dense and front-loaded: the BoJ Summary of Opinions on 10 August, Japanese Q2 GDP in the week of 17 August, the July trade balance on 19 August, the July national CPI on 20 August and the MoF intervention disclosure in the final week — against only Swiss July CPI and PMI on the base leg, both of which skew franc-negative anyway. Conviction rests on three things that make this more than a coin flip: the carry sign is arithmetic rather than forecast, the positioning asymmetry is measured rather than inferred, and the trend break in this specific cross is complete rather than partial. Actionability is good on carry and structure but constrained by liquidity — this is a thin cross where gap risk exceeds what 8% realised volatility implies.

Because the SNB has no communication event before 24 September, any hawkish revelation here moves the differential in one direction only.

catalysts.event: Reserve Bank of Australia policy decision
catalysts.rationale: A hold at 4.35% sustains the widest carry gap in the complex and confirms the carry-on regime that suppresses both legs of this cross roughly equally. It matters for CHF/JPY only as a regime read: a hawkish surprise deepens the carry-on environment and keeps both funding currencies pinned, while a dovish surprise is the first crack in the regime and would favour the yen leg on positioning.

catalysts.event: Japan July trade balance (MoF customs basis)
catalysts.rationale: June delivered a JPY 406.9bn deficit against a JPY 120bn consensus on record imports of JPY 11.34tn with mineral fuel imports up 41.9%. Because Brent fell 13% from USD 105.32 on 23 July to USD 91.82 on 27 July, the July bill should improve, which removes the most visible bullish-pair datapoint. This is the one release that speaks directly to the terms-of-trade differential — Japan's 83.95 against Switzerland's 100.60 — that is the pair's only structural bullish channel.

The most important single release in the tactical window. Tokyo July core printed 1.9% against a 1.7% consensus with core-core at 2.0%, and Tokyo leads the national series by roughly a month, so we expect national core at 1.8% or above against a consensus nearer 1.6%. Against a Swiss core of 0.3% that widens the inflation differential to -150bp and gives the BoJ its evidentiary basis for September, which is the direct route to a wider rate differential.

catalysts.event: Ministry of Finance monthly FX intervention disclosure (30 July to 27 August window)
catalysts.rationale: Confirms or refutes the JPY 8.45tn estimate for the 30 July operation, which is currently only an inference from BoJ current-account projections. A confirmed figure above JPY 10tn would establish this as Japan's second-largest operation on record and materially raise the perceived credibility of the official floor under the quote leg — which, combined with the SNB's one-directional pledge against franc strength, means both authorities are demonstrably capping this pair from opposite ends.

Q1 was +0.4% quarter-on-quarter on the sport-adjusted basis, and Q2 is the first quarter to capture the full effect of pre-tariff trade uncertainty, with Q2 real export growth of only +0.6% against +8.8% nominal. A print below 0.2% confirms the EY 0.6% annual forecast over the SNB's 'around 1%' and reinforces the growth differential against Japan's expected +0.8% annualised.

catalysts.event: FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.rationale: For a cross where both legs are funding currencies, a hawkish Fed deepens the carry-on regime and suppresses both roughly symmetrically, so the first-order effect nets out. The second-order effect is bearish for the pair: a hawkish Fed pushes USD/JPY toward the 160-164 zone in which the MoF has demonstrated it intervenes, which is an official yen bid with no franc equivalent. Net ambiguous with a mild bearish skew.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting
catalysts.rationale: The single largest scheduled event of the strategic window and the meeting Ueda pointed at when he said the Board would 'debate our policy from our next meeting onward'. A 25bp hike to 1.25% widens the bilateral differential from -100bp to -125bp. Sequencing is the pair-specific insight: this falls six days before the SNB assessment, so the quote leg sets the tone and the base leg can only react to a differential that has already widened.

catalysts.event: SNB Monetary Policy Assessment and news conference
catalysts.rationale: The largest scheduled Swiss event and the base leg's only chance to move the differential. The SNB revises its conditional inflation forecast — currently 0.6%/0.6%/0.7% and conditioned on 0.00% throughout — for the first time since the energy shock re-intensified. An upward revision above 0.9% for 2027 restores franc optionality and is bullish for the pair; a downward revision toward 0.4% revives negative-rate speculation and is bearish.

catalysts.event: Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs extend to all non-Annex-III Swiss importers
catalysts.rationale: The 15% capped rate took effect on 31 July for the seventeen Annex III companies and captures all remaining importers from this date. Pharmaceuticals are Switzerland's largest export category to the United States, so this is the point at which the tariff drag becomes economy-wide and begins to compress the Swiss surplus that anchors the pair's structural bullish case in Factor 5.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan MPM with quarterly Outlook Report
catalysts.rationale: Cumulative hike probability by this meeting is roughly 44-60% depending on the source, and the accompanying Outlook Report will show whether FY2027 core CPI is revised above the current 2.4% as energy subsidies roll off. This is the confirming event for the strategic thesis: if the differential has not widened by 30 October, the tactical squeeze becomes a completed episode with nothing structural behind it.

catalysts.event: SNB assessment and December MPR; BoJ MPM (18 December)
catalysts.rationale: The two banks meet eight days apart with the SNB first for the only time in the window. The SNB's December MPR is where its residual hawkish premium is paid or unwound, and the BoJ's December meeting carries an OIS-implied rate of 1.21%, roughly 81-84% cumulative probability of one hike. Both events fall immediately around the 31 December cross-currency basis turn, which raises the carrying cost of both legs simultaneously and historically squeezes the more crowded one — here the yen.

invalidators.condition: CHF/JPY closes above the 100-day moving average at 200.81 for three consecutive sessions with no further Japanese official intervention
invalidators.mechanism: The pair-specific technical break that converts systematic capital from buyer to seller of the cross would be fully reversed, restoring the bullish moving-average stack and signalling that the market has tested and dismissed the official floor under the quote leg in this specific cross rather than merely in USD/JPY
invalidators.monitor_indicator: CHF/JPY daily close versus the 100-day SMA at 200.805 and the 200-day at 200.993

invalidators.condition: Brent crude sustains above USD 115 per barrel for ten consecutive trading days
invalidators.mechanism: Japan imports roughly 99% of its oil against Switzerland's diversified and smaller exposure, so the terms-of-trade differential — already 83.95 against 100.60 — widens catastrophically for the quote leg and overwhelms a 100bp rate differential; this is the one channel in which both currencies are hurt but one is hurt roughly twice as hard
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Brent front month (FRED DCOILBRENTEU) alongside Japanese monthly mineral fuel import values
invalidators.monitor_frequency: Daily for Brent, monthly for imports

invalidators.condition: The Bank of Japan holds at both the 18 September and 30 October meetings with no upgrade to guidance and December OIS-implied falls below 1.10%
invalidators.mechanism: The bilateral differential then stays pinned at -100bp with no widening path, which removes the entire tactical and strategic rate case in a pair where the SNB cannot narrow the gap from its side since it is already at zero
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Three-month TONA futures and the OIS-implied post-December rate

invalidators.condition: The combined CFTC leveraged-fund and asset-manager yen net short falls below 80,000 contracts while CHF/JPY remains above 194.00
invalidators.mechanism: That is the precise signature of a squeeze completed without a trend: the pair-specific fuel that made the positioning differential a bearish signal has discharged, the franc leg has no equivalent short to fade, and the cross reverts to the range-bound funding-versus-funding behaviour that characterised it for the twelve months before July
invalidators.monitor_indicator: CFTC Commitments of Traders, Japanese yen, leveraged funds plus asset managers, against CHF/JPY spot

invalidators.condition: The 30-year JGB exceeds 4.25% while CHF/JPY simultaneously trades above 198.00
invalidators.mechanism: That combination is the definitive confirmation that Japanese yields are a sovereign credit premium rather than a policy premium — the exact configuration that produced a 122bp JGB rise alongside a 1.90% CHF/JPY gain over the past twelve months — meaning the pair is being priced on the 150-percentage-point debt differential rather than the 100bp rate differential
invalidators.monitor_indicator: MoF constant-maturity 30-year JGB yield alongside CHF/JPY spot

invalidators.condition: Swiss headline CPI prints at or above 1.0% year-on-year with SFSO core inflation 1 above 0.6% for two consecutive months
invalidators.mechanism: It would restore the base currency's policy optionality that the SNB has publicly abolished, forcing the market to price a genuine 2027 Swiss tightening and closing the bilateral differential from the base leg — the one direction the current thesis assumes is impossible
invalidators.monitor_indicator: SFSO Swiss CPI, headline and core inflation 1

invalidators.condition: The SNB announces large-scale intervention against franc strength exceeding CHF 15bn of sight-deposit accumulation in a four-week window while the Ministry of Finance publicly steps back from yen buying
invalidators.mechanism: The two-sided official cap that is the pair's most distinctive structural feature would become one-sided in the opposite direction, removing the asymmetry on which a substantial part of the Factor 6 bearish case rests
invalidators.monitor_indicator: SNB weekly sight deposits versus MoF monthly intervention disclosures

signposts.indicator: BoJ-SNB policy differential and the OIS-implied BoJ rate after 18 December
signposts.current_level: differential -100bp (BoJ 1.00%, SNB 0.00%); December OIS-implied BoJ rate 1.21%, i.e. 21bp cumulative priced
signposts.confirms_if: December-implied rises above 1.30%, or September hike probability exceeds 50% on both public representations, taking the projected differential beyond -125bp
signposts.invalidates_if: December-implied falls below 1.10% or September probability drops below 20%
signposts.bilateral_importance: This matters more for CHF/JPY than for any other cross of either currency because the SNB is pinned at the zero bound and therefore cannot narrow the gap from its side — the differential is a one-variable function of BoJ pricing, which is not true of USD/JPY, EUR/CHF or any other major cross of either leg
signposts.frequency: Daily, with step-changes around BoJ publications

signposts.indicator: CHF/JPY spot versus the 199.25 broken range floor and the 200.81-200.99 moving-average cluster
signposts.current_level: spot 195.05; 50d 199.702, 100d 200.805, 200d 200.993 — below all three, bearishly stacked; range floor 199.25 broken
signposts.confirms_if: Every rally attempt caps below 199.25 and the pair establishes a monthly close below 190.00
signposts.invalidates_if: Three consecutive daily closes above 200.81, or a weekly close above 200.99 restoring the bullish stack
signposts.bilateral_importance: Unlike USD/JPY, where the JPY dossier notes the 200-day held and the break is partial, this cross has completed a full three-average break — so it is the cleanest available chart expression of the CHF-weak/JPY-strong combination and the place where systematic flow has already flipped
signposts.frequency: Daily, assessed on Friday and month-end closes

signposts.indicator: The CFTC positioning spread: JPY net short versus CHF net short
signposts.current_level: JPY combined -185,047 contracts (28 July report, ≈4th percentile) against CHF combined -46,455 (≈52nd percentile) — a spread of roughly 139,000 contracts
signposts.confirms_if: The JPY short shrinks by 40,000 or more over two reports while CHF/JPY trades below 192.50, showing covering is driving the cross
signposts.invalidates_if: The JPY short falls below 80,000 with the pair still above 194.00 (squeeze spent, no trend), or the CHF short deepens beyond -70,000 contracts (the franc leg becomes the crowded one)
signposts.bilateral_importance: The single-leg CFTC series tell you nothing about this pair; only the spread reveals that the pair-implied speculative position is long CHF/JPY, and the four-to-one open-interest asymmetry (423,796 vs 107,866 contracts) means the squeeze capacity sits entirely in the quote leg
signposts.frequency: Weekly, Friday 15:30 ET, as at the prior Tuesday

signposts.indicator: Brent crude alongside the Japan-Switzerland terms-of-trade gap
signposts.current_level: Brent USD 91.82 (27 July, down from USD 105.32 on 23 July); Japan terms of trade 83.95, Switzerland 100.60 — a 16.65-point gap
signposts.confirms_if: Brent sustains below USD 90 and Japanese terms of trade recover above 88, narrowing the gap below 13 points
signposts.invalidates_if: Brent above USD 115 for ten sessions, or Japanese terms of trade fall below 80 toward the 69.80 record low
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the only channel that reverses the thesis quickly, and it exists solely because both currencies are energy importers of radically different intensity — a distinction invisible in either standalone dossier, where oil is simply 'negative' for both
signposts.frequency: Daily for Brent, monthly for terms of trade

signposts.indicator: The two-sided official cap: SNB sight deposits versus MoF intervention disclosures
signposts.current_level: SNB sight deposits of domestic banks CHF 442.66bn (week to 24 July), +CHF 9.6bn over three months; MoF 2026 interventions ≈JPY 20tn (official JPY 11,734.9bn for April-May plus an estimated JPY 8.45tn on 30 July)
signposts.confirms_if: SNB sight deposits continue rising modestly (SNB selling francs) while the MoF confirms an operation above JPY 10tn or executes a second tranche
signposts.invalidates_if: SNB sight deposits fall more than CHF 10bn over four weeks (SNB selling reserves, i.e. supporting the franc) while the MoF publicly steps back from yen buying
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the structural feature unique to CHF/JPY in the entire G10 matrix — two central banks whose one-directional reaction functions both cap the same pair from opposite ends. No other cross has an official seller of the base currency and an official buyer of the quote currency simultaneously
signposts.frequency: SNB weekly (Mondays); MoF monthly (end of month)

signposts.indicator: Gold as the haven-complex arbiter between the two legs
signposts.current_level: XAU/USD 4,054.45 (31 July), -12.14% over three months and -17.94% over six from a February peak of 5,277.88
signposts.confirms_if: Gold remains below 4,400, keeping the debasement-and-uncertainty demand function dormant, which suppresses the franc's shared haven bid while leaving the yen's positioning-and-intervention bid intact
signposts.invalidates_if: Gold sustains a break above 4,600, signalling structural re-engagement of the haven complex, which historically pulls the franc higher through a shared demand function that the yen does not share
signposts.bilateral_importance: In a haven-versus-haven cross, gold is the tiebreaker. The franc correlates to gold through a shared debasement premium; the yen does not, and in 2026 has actually been hurt by the energy component of geopolitical risk

signposts.indicator: CHF/JPY 20-day realised volatility as the regime gauge
signposts.current_level: ~8.0% annualised (computed from supplied daily OHLC to 5 August), against ~4.1% measured to 29 July and ~5.7% on a five-day basis
signposts.confirms_if: Realised holds above 7.0%, indicating the low-volatility range regime that dominated the pair for twelve months has genuinely broken and trend-following flow can persist
signposts.invalidates_if: Realised falls back below 5.0% with the pair holding a 193-199 band, which would mean the July move was an event spike inside an intact range rather than a regime change
signposts.bilateral_importance: This matters more here than in any other yen or franc cross because CHF/JPY is documented as a range-bound, low-liquidity funding-versus-funding pair that ranks sixth by European-session volume — volatility persistence is the specific condition under which a directional thesis in this cross survives

assumptions: Price data is the source of truth for all price-derived metrics. Spot of 195.05459 (5 August close), the 52-week range of 175.868-204.42917, the 67th range percentile, the 1M/3M/6M/1Y performance figures, and the 50-day (199.70164), 100-day (200.80504) and 200-day (200.99265) moving averages are all taken directly from the supplied Twelve Data series and are not reconciled against web sources. The CHF dossier's derived CHF/JPY level of 196.24 for 31 July diverges 119 pips from the price data's 195.05 for the same session, attributable to different snapshot times; all levels in this report use the price data.

Realised volatility is computed by us, not sourced. The 20-day figure of approximately 8.0%, the pre-event figure of approximately 4.1% and the five-day figure of approximately 5.7% are calculated from close-to-close log-adjacent percentage returns in the supplied series, annualised at √252. The supplied series contains some weekend and holiday fills that compress measured volatility slightly; the direction and magnitude of the doubling are robust to that, the precise levels are not.

CHF/JPY implied volatility, risk reversals and vol term structure are NOT OBSERVED. No free source publishes an ATM strip, a skew or a term structure for this cross. The 3M implied estimates used are the CHF dossier's zero-correlation proxy of 8.49% (which overstates true cross vol) and the JPY dossier's estimate of 7.0%. The conclusion that the net cross skew is approximately flat is an inference from observed single-leg skews and is not a measured cross-skew observation. No IV percentile can be computed.

CHF/JPY forward points are DERIVED, not quoted. No source publishes CHF/JPY forwards. The cross-implied path of approximately +0.84% annualised is constructed by differencing the two dossiers' observed USD-leg forward-implied rates, which assumes the cross basis is additive and that both dossiers' snapshots are contemporaneous. The resulting outrights are our calculation from the supplied spot, not market quotes.

Cross-currency basis for this pair is unobtainable. Neither the 3M CHF/JPY cross basis nor the 3M USD/CHF and USD/JPY bases were obtainable from free sources this cycle. Factor 10 is therefore assessed without its primary instrument at both horizons and its confidence is capped at 48 and 45 for that reason.

Valuation is presented on two incompatible bases and neither is an absolute PPP estimate. The CHF dossier's +55.73% deviation with an implied fair value of 126.0 is a ratio of BIS real-effective indices and is presented as an ordinal signal only. The JPY dossier's -7.7% figure with an implied fair value of 181.13 is more defensible for a bilateral comparison and is the figure relied upon. Neither is a tradeable target.

Positioning figures are as-at different dates. The CHF leg is the 21 July CFTC report; the JPY leg is given at both 21 July and 28 July. We use the 28 July yen figure for the extremity argument and note the eleven-day staleness of the franc leg, which is the specific reason Factor 4 tactical confidence is 70 rather than higher.

Bilateral trade is taken directly from the injected IMF DOTS block and not re-estimated, noting the standard mirror-statistics discrepancy between Swiss- and Japanese-reported figures; we use the Swiss-reported net figure of USD 1.6bn and treat the flow channel as immaterial for spot.

Bilateral portfolio investment flows are a documented gap. No public series disaggregates Japanese portfolio holdings of Swiss securities or vice versa at usable frequency; FDI evidence cited is directional only.

Weight adjustments are documented with bilateral reasons, are each within ±0.05, and sum to exactly 1.00 at both horizons. Two of the four adjustments (the strategic boost to External Balance and both reductions to USD Liquidity) work against the report's directional conclusion, which is deliberate.

Stance-to-score mapping and conviction ladder: Bullish (pair rises) = +1, Neutral = 0, Bearish (pair falls) = -1; confidence-adjusted score = stance score × confidence / 100; weighted contribution = confidence-adjusted score × horizon weight. We adopt the CHF dossier's conviction ladder throughout for internal consistency, and flag that the strategic score of -0.1757 would map to conviction 3 rather than 2 on the JPY dossier's ladder.

Support and resistance levels are sourced from web technical analysis and cross-checked against the supplied price series where possible. Web-sourced levels published at spot above 202 are noted as stale and are not used as operative levels.

Bank forecast coverage for this specific pair is thin. Only one dated institutional recommendation on CHF/JPY was obtainable (Bank of America, June 2026), plus a September 2025 note from the same institution in the opposite direction. No 3M/6M/12M consensus grid exists for this cross, so the Where We Differ From Consensus section benchmarks against the derived forward curve as well as the single bank target.
